items.lbText:
Carrick says it is possible to restore former glory at Old Trafford with time and Unai Emery confirms Aston Villa contract talks

Arteta agreed Rice had strengthened his ball progression, and explained his thinking behind dropping the 27-year-old deeper. “We cannot restrict his qualities and his capacities,” Arteta said. “He can drop back, he can progress play. He can drop back, he can carry the ball, he can be incredible in transition.

“He can win duels. He can produce passes by arriving, by playing far, by crossing the ball left or right, it doesn’t matter. On set pieces [too], he’s got a lot to offer. His shooting ability from long range as well is something that we need to use more.” PA

Unai Emery has confirmed he has held talks over signing a new contract with a view to building a “stronger” project at Aston Villa.

On Wednesday, the day after Villa’s 3-0 Champions League defeat at Barcelona, the club said they had held a meeting to discuss their long-term strategy beyond 2029, when Emery’s deal is due to expire.

The manager been linked with several clubs, including Manchester United, but was involved with long-term talks, including with the chair, Nassef Sawiris.

Emery said: “My ambition is to keep our consistency and how we are improving and building lots of things positively. It is a huge challenge. They decided, speaking with us last year, to build a new stand to add more supporters at Villa Park. That is a clear step forward to get better.

“How we are increasing our budget each year, and revenue through our performance by playing in Europe and improving players, selling players, then buying young talented players, this is the process and ambition we should keep in the future.

“I had a good meeting with Nassef Sawiris, very good meeting, very positive. Let’s talk next week, trying to get everything we spoke about together. We were speaking about how we can set our project stronger with a deal, yes.” PA

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Lampard appreciation at Everton, Glasner sparking Forest fire, Zubimendi and Kroupi in spotlight and Carrick v Emery

Nothing better encapsulates the dysfunction that was Everton under Farhad Moshiri than the idea that an unknown vandal with a can of spray paint could influence the club’s managerial direction. “Pereira out, Lampard in” they daubed on a wall at Goodison Park when it appeared Vítor Pereira was in line to replace Rafael Benítez in 2022. Alarmed by fan protests, the Everton board opted instead for Frank Lampard and, while his tenure ended 12 months later with the club immersed in another relegation battle, there will be appreciation for the Coventry manager when he makes a first visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday. The connection between Lampard and Evertonians was genuine and a factor in keeping the club up in 2022. Both parties will be glad to see the other emerging stronger from those troubled times. Jack Grealish, meanwhile, will again be absent for Everton after his recent disciplinary breach, although the manager, David Moyes, said: “We will be working again with Jack soon.”

Everton v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times GMT)

v Tottenham, Saturday 12.30pm

items.title: Champions League review: comebacks, thrashings and a Mauritanian first
items.author: Jeff Rueter
items.content:
Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain flexed their muscles, Manchester United fought back and an unlikely star stole the show for AEK Athens

Still without the recovering Vincent Kompany, Bayern Munich are among the favorites to win the Champions League, which would be their first European title since 2019-20. Aaron Danks’ side produced a dominant display at the Metropolitano, playing Atlético Madrid off the field in a commanding 2-0 win. Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer made the difference, with Harry Kane providing Laimer with a fine assist in his first continental appearance since winning the Ballon d’Or. Bayern remain just outside the top eight, which guarantees automatic passage to the last 16, having won two and drawn two of their opening four matches.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain flexed their muscles, Manchester United fought back and an unlikely star stole the show for AEK Athens

Still without the recovering Vincent Kompany, Bayern Munich are among the favorites to win the Champions League , which would be their first European title since 2019-20. René Marić’s side produced a dominant display at the Metropolitano, playing Atlético Madrid off the field in a commanding 2-0 win. Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer made the difference, with Harry Kane providing Laimer with a fine assist in his first continental appearance since winning the Ballon d’Or. Bayern remain just outside the top eight, which guarantees automatic passage to the last 16, having won two and drawn two of their opening four matches.

It was also a massive week for Michael Carrick’s claim to the Manchester United job, as his side overturned a 2-0 half-time deficit to beat Roma 3-2 . United have now won two, drawn two and lost none, enough to enter the international break in the play-off places.

Villarreal manager Iñigo Pérez warned that if visiting Paris Saint-Germain “smell fear, they won’t forgive you”, and evidently his players must have reeked of it. The reigning European champions redefined “scoring for fun” with an early onslaught, putting four goals past the sinking Yellow Submarine inside 17 minutes. PSG ultimately cruised to a remarkable 6-0 thrashing, with their five different scorers led by Fabián Ruiz, who scored a brace.

Inter got their campaign back on track with a commanding 3-0 win away at Feyenoord, a strong response to their defeat in the Milan derby. An eighth-minute strike from Yann Bisseck put the 2025 runners-up in front and they never looked back. “Football doesn’t always go to plan, but you have to respond, make the right changes and find a way to get back on track,” Inter coach Cristian Chivu said afterwards. One such change may be giving Djed Spence a greater role. Named player of the match on Tuesday after providing the assist for Bisseck’s opener, Spence has seldom featured in his first season, having made his first Serie A start only in Saturday’s defeat to Milan.

Como continue to win matches, as well as hearts and minds, and followed their 4-1 victory over Manchester United with an even more emphatic performance. Lens were the latest victims, with Como thrashing the French side 9-1. Cesc Fàbregas’s team continue to defy expectations in their first Champions League campaign. They sit fourth in Serie A and the Champions League tables.

Aboubakary Koita, AEK Athens . While far from a vintage Real Madrid side, or even a vintage José Mourinho version of one, Los Blancos headed to Athens brimming with confidence. Madrid had won all six of their matches since play resumed after the international break, including a statement victory at the Camp Nou in late October. And yet, they seemed to have no answer for a player representing a nation ranked 110th in the world by Fifa.

Koita kept Madrid’s full-backs on their heels throughout a tireless 90-minute shift for AEK Athens . Having taken just two shots in his first 180 minutes of this season’s Champions League, the 28-year-old winger put Madrid on notice early on Wednesday. Koita collected the ball on the edge of the penalty area in the 12th minute and bore down on Marc Cucurella. He cut inside, twisting the left-back out of position, before driving a powerful effort between Thibaut Courtois and his near post.

It was the first Champions League goal scored by a player from Mauritania.

Madrid fought hard to equalize, with Jude Bellingham having one effort ruled out for a narrow offside before his clever left-footed finish caught Alberto Brignoli by surprise. The hosts held firm until the 75th minute, when Koita drew defenders towards him as he drifted towards the left corner before spotting a run from his left-back, Stavros Pilios. Koita threaded the ball into the defender’s path and Pilios coolly slotted it past Courtois.

Ultimately, Madrid had too much talent for AEK’s defence. Kylian Mbappé made no mistake, scoring his team’s second equalizer three minutes after Pilios’s effort. Federico Valverde had no intention of giving the hosts a happy ending, powering a long-range effort across goal and beyond the diving Brignoli. Nonetheless, it was a hard-earned winner forced by Koita’s brilliance at the other end.

Koita’s night ended on a sour note. Furious after being brought down as the final whistle blew, he earned a red card for telling the referee to “fuck off”, then remained on the pitch to plead his case.

An impressive hat-trick in its own way: a historic goal, an assist and a red card.

Recent history has cast Fenerbahçe as the ultimate nearly team, finishing second in every Süper Lig campaign since 2021-22. A poor start to the season prompted İsmail Kartal’s resignation, leaving Dirk Kuyt, who had joined the club only in June as Kartal’s assistant, to become caretaker manager.

Kuyt’s first European match in charge carried even greater significance given the visitors: Liverpool , with whom he became a legend.

“As soon as the draw came up, as a technical member of the staff I was really excited because everyone knows how much Fenerbahçe and Liverpool mean to me,” Kuyt said on the eve of the match. “Of course tomorrow will be a very, very special occasion for me. But at the stage we are in, I’m not the important person. It’s the club.”

A job well done for the club, then, as Fenerbahçe stormed back from 2-1 down with 20 minutes remaining. Former Derby County academy product Archie Brown made Liverpool pay, scoring the equalizer before setting up Vedat Muriqi’s winner. The defeat was Andoni Iraola’s first in European competition, although Liverpool remain comfortably placed to advance.…

items.title: The international break is almost here: so wave goodbye to your players, and maybe your manager | Max Rushden
items.author: Max Rushden
items.content:
What used to be a time to reset is now a time to rehire, and Michael Carrick is not the only Premier League manager looking over his shoulder

Perhaps the most telling moment of Manchester United’s comeback against Roma was at the final whistle. The camera focused on Michael Carrick, who shook the hand of Gian Piero Gasperini before looking around trying to remember what you’re meant to do after a victory. The camera then cut to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, clapping with two of the most ashen faces you could imagine – as if it was a minute’s applause in the 87th minute for a lifelong, octogenarian fan who died peacefully in his sleep earlier in the week (most probably not at a United game but you couldn’t rule it out).

Of course, there are rules about smiling when you are involved with a failing football club. Players can’t be seen to be enjoying themselves in the week after a defeat, managers have to be earnest at almost all times, apart from when a journalist’s phone goes off at a press conference – a moment of sporting hilarity on a par with a pigeon landing on Centre Court.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
What used to be a time to reset is now a time to rehire, and Michael Carrick is not the only Premier League manager looking over his shoulder

P erhaps the most telling moment of Manchester United’s comeback against Roma was at the final whistle. The camera focused on Michael Carrick, who shook the hand of Gian Piero Gasperini before looking around trying to remember what you’re meant to do after a victory. The camera then cut to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, clapping with two of the most ashen faces you could imagine – as if it was a minute’s applause in the 87th minute for a lifelong, octogenarian fan who died peacefully in his sleep earlier in the week (most probably not at a United game but you couldn’t rule it out).

Of course, there are rules about smiling when you are involved with a failing football club. Players can’t be seen to be enjoying themselves in the week after a defeat, managers have to be earnest at almost all times, apart from when a journalist’s phone goes off at a press conference – a moment of sporting hilarity on a par with a pigeon landing on Centre Court.

So it stands to reason that Wilcox and Berrada were right not to be shirtless, swirling their Ineos gilets around their heads at full time. Same goes for the other one, also known as head of recruitment Christopher Vivell, who has borrowed Rodri’s cloak of invisibility for this whole saga. Of all the free passes going in the game at the moment, he is playing a blinder.

But were they so solemn because they’d just agreed terms with Unai Emery at half-time ( don’t sue me, Nassef – that was clumsy, wrong and tongue-in-cheek, keep on keeping on, keep on ascending, lots of love xoxoxox)? You couldn’t blame them. And 45 minutes later United are BACK. It was an astonishing turnaround. Where has that front-foot, aggressive football been?

There was quite a lot of luck - a soft penalty missed and retaken, a wild miskick, Roma missing a hatful of chances before the break. All those moments could have signalled the end.

It is unlikely that the penalty is Carrick’s Mark Robins/Adrian Heath moment, but win at home against Aston Villa on Sunday and it is not beyond the realms of possibility that he turns the season around. It is also not beyond the realms of possibility that United are so badly run that they get a lucky win over Villa, stick with Carrick and revert to what we’ve seen and end up surviving, Spurs-style, on the last day.

You will have heard every pundit mention the hierarchy waiting for the international break to make the call. Perhaps Sir Jim Ratcliffe saw how much content Manchester City gave us in the previous one and wants the column inches.

But it isn’t only Carrick who will be sweating while watching a repeat of Pointless Celebrities or whatever else is in place of Match of the Day when the Premier League has a week off. There are realistically five managers who may not be in place when we all return.

From the bottom up: Régis Le Bris at Sunderland , who host good-at-attacking, bad-at-defending Chelsea on Sunday. This would be a classic case of victim of your own success. Qualify for Europe for the first time in more than 50 years, fail to recruit adequately, then chuck out the manager who achieved that success. But if Bromley can get rid of Andy Woodman, anything is possible.

If you want evidence all is not well at the Stadium of Light, a friend recently took a posh taxi in Yarm that had No 34 embroidered into all the seats, plus three screens and the night sky on the ceiling. If Granit Xhaka is selling his personalised Renault Espace, perhaps Le Bris has lost the dressing room. Either that or Granit’s just embroidered a Hummer. Look, I don’t have many sources, so I can only work with what I’ve got.

In 19th position: Oliver Glasner and Nottingham Forest . A tricky home game with Manchester City* late on Saturday afternoon. His “too many compromises” comments reminded me of a baffling perfume advert from the 2010s where a man announces at a press conference that he’s no longer going to be the man he’s expected to be any more, ignoring the fact none of us know what he was expected to be in the first place. Was Glasner talking about the players or the looming presence in the directors’ box? Is Evangelos Marinakis insisting on taking the rondos? Or has Glasner spent the past three months telling Liam Delap to try to take a bit off it and opt for placement, with Delap resolute in using every bit of his “shot power – 99” at every opportunity?

In 18th: Pierre Sage at Crystal Palace. He doesn’t have a lot going for him. I can’t speak for everyone, but let me try. No one watched how good Lens were last season under Sage and they appear worse now if shipping 9 (nine) at home to Como is anything to go by. So Sage appearing unknown and dour leads to all manner of pundits announcing how uninspiring he is. Perhaps he’s a hoot at training. Palace have sold a lot of good players and replaced them with not as good players, which feels like a risk. Yet you fear for him, you really do.

And then there’s Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle. Could defeat at Fulham on Saturday spell the end for him? The common theme appears to be selling the spine of a team and expecting a new guy to deliver. And yet there is a disconnect between him and the fans. We call for managers to be given time, but what if you give time to the wrong guy? Jaissle has a good reputation but even geordies still completely invested in the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund project probably didn’t watch too many of his Al-Ahli games over the past three years.…

items.lbText:
Madrid hope to bring in forward during January

United to consider legal action if they feel rules broken

Real Madrid are closing in on signing JJ Gabriel, though Manchester United will consider legal action if the club believe any rules have been broken.

Madrid have offered the 16-year-old forward a multi-year contract and, subject to final talks, hope to bring him to the club in January. Gabriel is registered with United’s academy until the end of the season and it is understood the club have yet to be contacted by the player’s camp or Madrid regarding the proposed move.

Madrid intend to sign Gabriel via a Fifa loophole that allows clubs in the European Union to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have an EU passport, which Gabriel is eligible to acquire through both his parents.

Fifa would have to sign this off and United are on alert regarding any potential breach of regulations. A compensation fee would be due to United if Gabriel joined Madrid or any other team. Madrid have been approached for comment.

Gabriel walked out on United in September and is believed to be training in Spain. A move to Madrid offers the prospect of progression to senior football via their B team, Castilla, who play in the regionalised Spanish third tier.

Gabriel played in a pre-season friendly for United against Atlético Madrid in Stockholm in August at the age of 15 and had been training with the first team. If he had not informed United of his wish to depart , he would have been in Michael Carrick’s squad for the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on 16 September. Had Gabriel featured, he would have become the youngest player in the club’s history.

Gabriel last season became the youngest winner of United’s academy player of the year award and was the Premier League’s Under-18 player of the season.

items.lbText:
Full-back believes 3-2 win can transform season

United were booed off by supporters at half-time

Diogo Dalot believes Manchester United’s comeback against Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday can transform their troubled season and, as importantly, showed unhappy supporters that the players care.

The Glazer family, who have owned United since 2005 and loaded £1.2bn of debt on to the club, continue to be the focus for fan anger and there was yet another protest against them before kick-off at Old Trafford, with thousands of green-and-gold balloons released from the Stretford End. The home crowd sang anti-Glazer songs and threw tennis balls on to the pitch when the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds, to symbolise the year 2005. The team have seven points from their opening nine games of the Premier League season, their worst start since 1987-88.

The players have also been criticised, with the Stretford End turning on them as they left the pitch after the recent 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth . The fans had previously serenaded the manager, Michael Carrick, who they back to the hilt.

Dalot was the last player to depart that day. He walked off slowly and looked defiant in the face of the jeers. It was a much happier story for him and the team against Roma, with Matheus Cunha’s two late goals sealing a 3-2 victory. United had been booed off at half-time as they trailed 2-0. Bruno Fernandes started the revival when he scored with a retaken penalty.

“These moments are really tough, I’m not going to lie,” Dalot said. “Unfortunately, I’ve had a few moments like this in the past and the only way for us to get out is by winning football games. Nights like this [against Roma] give you an extra confidence that makes you believe you can create these moments – not just for us but for the fans. And it’s important from everyone around the club feeling that we care, that we want to turn this around. I think we showed, especially in the second 45 minutes, that we really want to turn this around.”

Dalot, now into his ninth season as a United player, is a symbol of the club’s difficulties; the muddled thinking. Forced to play out of position at left-back as the only specialist in the position – Luke Shaw – is injured, he has given his all. But with imbalances and weaknesses elsewhere in the defence, the Portuguese’s best efforts have not always been enough. The decision of the United hierarchy not to sign any defensive reinforcements over the summer continues to dumbfound.

Dalot, who has been a target for social media abuse, was a part of the dismal first-half performance against Roma. Carrick took a risk by asking him to push high up the field at the outset, knowing that any turnovers could lead to problems. Which is precisely what happened for the first goal after Kobbie Mainoo lost the ball in central midfield. Roma moved easily into the space that United had vacated at left-back to score through Matias Soulé. Their winning of the penalty for the second goal also came as Dalot was committed forward.

He was asked whether Carrick had told him to play so high. “Yes, obviously,” Dalot replied. “We knew that they were going to play man-to-man but that requires some things that we need to avoid – especially losing balls in the middle because we knew that we’re going to be too open. Obviously, after the second goal, we tried to fix it straight away. I think we balanced a little bit more the game [after that].”

To borrow a phrase from Thomas Tuchel, United played “fuck it football” in the second half. Tuchel said Argentina had adopted this approach against his team in the World Cup semi-final as they trailed 1-0. Argentina scored late goals to win 2-1 .

“If you analyse it really cold, we had nothing more to lose,” the 27-year-old said. “I mean, that’s the unfortunate situation we are in. So we just had to really go at it. In the first five, 10 minutes of the second half, we were winning duels, we were on the front foot. The crowd came with us and pushed us forward.

“Once you create that energy inside the stadium, it’s really tough for the opponents to create even a chance. That’s the biggest thing we need to get out of this game – when we play like this, when you have the right attitude, when the fans really believe that we are there, we can be a very strong team. It is not just the manager, everyone is under pressure. We felt it, obviously. Nights like this can change momentum, they can change seasons.”

United host Aston Villa on Sunday and will need to show the same resilience. “The key message from us [during half-time against Roma] … it’s like we’re getting disappointed too quick,” Dalot said. “Every moment in the game where it doesn’t go the way that we want, it’s like we let ourselves down a little bit. That’s the momentum we need to change.”

items.title: Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames
items.author: Nick Ames at Old Trafford
items.content:
There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

items.lbText:
There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

Until United are equipped to repeat their second 45 minutes on a weekly basis, which requires systemic change in departments far outside the technical area, even if Carrick’s head will surely be first on the block, nobody is likely to deliver them from ongoing psychodrama. History may tell that his heavily maligned players were fruitlessly raging against the dying of the light in blowing Roma out of the water. But their achievement here was worth savouring for its discreet brilliance and, perhaps, the wholesome powers that ultimately wrought it.

Kobbie Mainoo had been introduced as “Manchester born and bred”, to obligatory cheers, when the teams were read out. Any emotional heartstring is worth plucking on at the moment but there was something grounding about seeing the midfielder, largely injured over the past month and an onlooker while his colleagues’ fortunes spiralled, return to the starting XI. Mainoo was far from alone in enduring a tentative, twitchy, flustered first half but was caught flat-footed when Marten de Roon mugged him near halfway, setting in train the move that exposed an execrably organised backline for Matías Soulé’s opener.

At 2-0, another crossfield ball from the left having triggered United’s defence into recidivism, Mainoo attempted to raise spirits by surging through the middle on his own and spraying the ball right under pressure. There was no more nourishing gruel on offer than this; the only nagging glimmer of possibility was that Roma, for all their broad control, did not look like the kind of side that would withstand any gale that came their way.

When Carlos Baleba, eye-catching in phases but loose in possession, pulled up with Bryan Mbeumo ready for a tap-in, the notes of misery deepened. But the subsequent introduction of Youri Tielemans, in his element against opponents whose intensity was evidently sagging, created angles and spaces that had previously seemed figments of the mind. United were fortunate when Bruno Fernandes converted his soft, twice-taken penalty; they were gifted parity when Leonardo Balerdi’s air-kick afforded Matheus Cunha a chance he could barely miss. The die, though, had long been cast through their waves of slick, insistent pressure.

So it fell for Mainoo and another academy product, Shea Lacey, to tee up the coup de grace. Lacey hails from Liverpool but there is no need to whisper that: his credentials since childhood have firmly passed muster. While Lisandro Martínez was lightly booed on to the pitch in the 75th minute, Lacey arrived with him to raptures. How poetic it was that Mainoo, speeding up an attack before quickly shifting the ball right, and the mesmerising Lacey, should complete the revival.

Lacey’s jink inside and left-footed pass whipped into Cunha were genuinely breathtaking. So was the finish and so, too, the reaction. Few do it quite like an Old Trafford crowd on a European night. This is still a citadel like no other, even if its strains nowadays alternate between dubbing Mainoo unplayable and impolitely requesting the Glazers to make haste back across the Atlantic.

The contradictions fizzed everywhere on this thick, still night. Earlier on Wednesday Carrick will doubtless have been spared the news that sacking season had already visited the Ineos football empire. At this point Jim Ratcliffe’s sporting citadels are more akin to a line of Dickensian rubbish heaps, their proprietor a modern-day golden dustman, and the plug had been pulled on Luka Elsner and United’s hapless junior sibling, Lausanne Sport. They are bottom of the Swiss top flight and results, a club statement explained, had been the determining factor in the manager’s demise.

They have not exactly helped Carrick either . Mainoo had claimed in a transactionally toned pre-match press conference that United could be “one win away” from changing the shape and scope of their season. In reality all that can be guaranteed about whatever occurs next is the sheer theatre of it. Of course it is Unai Emery, discussion whose suitability or otherwise for any United vacancy has brought surprising ramifications, who walks into this perplexing cocktail of loathing and unconditional support this weekend. Carrick will need the football to perform him a few more favours yet.

items.title: ‘I wasn’t performing’: Bruno Fernandes says Carrick was right to drop him after criticism
items.author: Nick Ames at Old Trafford
items.content:
• ‘If it was punishment for the words, it was right’

  • Carrick hails ‘magical’ Old Trafford after comeback win

A twice-taken penalty from ­Fernandes set United’s revival from 2-0 down in motion, two goals from Matheus Cunha ultimately sealing a win that could yet save the embattled Carrick’s job.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
‘If it was punishment for the words, it was right’

Carrick hails ‘magical’ Old Trafford after comeback win

Bruno Fernandes said Michael ­Carrick was correct to drop him last month as he reflected on a remarkable Manchester United comeback win against Roma at Old Trafford.

A twice-taken penalty from ­Fernandes set United’s revival from 2-0 down in motion, two goals from Matheus Cunha ultimately sealing a win that could yet save the embattled Carrick’s job.

Fernandes had been dropped after their previous Champions League game, a 4-1 humbling at Como , ­having criticised the manager’s ­tactics in a post-match interview. He was an unused substitute against Bournemouth in their next fixture and said he accepted the short-lived demotion.

“The manager took a decision of making myself on the bench because I wasn’t performing. And that’s fair,” Fernandes said. “Everyone felt like that was a punishment for the words that I had [after Como]. And if it was, it was right.

“The manager makes the ­decisions. I have to accept it. I have to go forward with that. It doesn’t change the belief I have in the manager, the staff and every player at this club. And it doesn’t change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me.”

Fernandes attempted to take the attention away from Carrick after United’s first win in 10 games, which was sealed amid a raucous atmosphere pockmarked by protests against the club’s ownership. They narrowly avoided completing their longest winless run during a single season since March 1978.

“We don’t need to save anyone’s job,” he said. “The club needed that win. The players needed that win. It is something we needed as a group of players and staff. We have been working so hard to get out of this situation together.”

A satisfied Carrick hailed the magic of Old Trafford after United’s rip-roaring second half. “I don’t like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do in history and what’s gone before them too much, but it’s there,” he said. “This place does magical things, it’s done it before and it’ll do it over and over again at some point in the future. There’s just something in this place that when we do have these types of night, we do it the hard way.”

Carrick heaped praise on the 19-year-old substitute Shea Lacey, who brilliantly set up Cunha’s winner on his 10th senior appearance. “We love him to bits,” he said. “He’s a great young man, he’s desperate to do well, he’s got great ability. He’s got that little glint in his eye, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like.”

items.lbText:
Michael Carrick enjoyed one of his finest nights as a Manchester United player in the Champions League against Roma, scoring twice in a 7-1 win in the quarter-final, second leg in 2007. The re-run here was all about his managerial survival at the club.

The situation looked impossibly grim for him at half-time. Amid an atmosphere of continued fan anger towards the United ownership, Carrick’s team had been implausibly bad. Roma took a 2-0 lead into the break and the truth was that the scoreline greatly flattered United.

What happened next was a fightback for the ages. For Carrick, it might even have topped 2007. United’s defending had been so loose, so generous. But they finally showed the other side to their game – the one about attacking punch; derring-do. They found a solution to their woes at the back. Keep the ball in the other half.

Matheus Cunha was the hero and it said plenty about the chaos of this game, the wildness of the emotions, that he ended up being sent off for a second yellow card in the 90th minute for a lunge at Leonardo Balerdi.

Before that, he had supplemented a Bruno Fernandes penalty – which the captain converted after a retake – with a touch and finish following an error from Balerdi. Cunha’s second goal, which proved to be the winner, was hammered in off the near post after a pass from the substitute, Shea Lacey. Cunha’s first touch to control was a beauty.

The United support sing about having seen it all. This was just extraordinary. Can it save Carrick? He will go into Sunday’s Premier League game at home against Aston Villa with renewed belief.

The fragility of the United backline has been well documented. How the hierarchy decided that it did not need any reinforcements over the summer is beyond belief. With Luke Shaw still injured, Carrick was forced to persist with Diogo Dalot out of position at left-back.

Dalot pushed very high at the outset, which felt bold. It was plainly a demand from Carrick. Dalot’s positioning was pure folly on the opening Roma goal. The visitors transitioned quickly, far too quickly for United’s ponderous defence and when Rodrigo Mora looked up from the inside left, all he could see was Matías Soulé in acres of space on the opposite channel. Where was Dalot? Mora played the pass. Soulé took a touch and swept past the exposed Senne Lammens.

United’s defending for the second goal was even worse. Leny Yoro turned and ran back towards his own goal as Roma advanced up the left, and when the move appeared to have broken down for them around the United box, there was Harry Maguire to gift it back to Soulé with a dreadful miskick. Soulé dropped his shoulder and shot; the ball hit Ayden Heaven’s hand and Donyell Malen converted from the spot. Again, Dalot had been high up the pitch.

The mutiny could be felt before kick-off; the sounds of it heard. There were the green and gold balloons of protest against the Glazers. The relentless chants against the club’s owners. When the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds – or 2005; the year of the Glazer takeover – the Stretford End erupted in a planned move; hurling tennis balls down on to the pitch.

Moments earlier, a grisly Dalot error on the ball had almost led to Malen getting in for a third and the first half was just an ordeal for United. Roma were well organised in their 3-4-2-1 shape and they got in up the inside right time and again. They might have had many more before the interval; Mora, Malen and Soulé all went close.

United offered minimal resistance. They were so easy to play through. There was nervousness from them on the ball, heavy touches. A glaring lack of cohesion. What was the plan? When Bruno Fernandes had a half-chance on the edge of the box in the 43th minute, he could not sort out his feet and blazed high.

Carrick was in the last chance saloon during half-time. He had to have a simple demand of his players: show some fight. There had been no evidence of it in the first period. Yet United emerged with purpose.

Carrick lost Carlos Baleba in the 46th minute. The midfielder stormed into the Roma area and was about to shoot only to pull his hamstring. Then, United caught a break – two, actually – and the mood shifted sharply.

It was a soft penalty award for a push by Gianluca Mancini on Cunha after he played a give-and-go with Fernandes. But when United had that sinking feeling after Fernandes saw his kick saved by Devis Vásquez, they were reprieved when the referee, Jesús Gil Manzano, ordered a retake for encroachment. Fernandes lashed it home.

United came alive. Bryan Mbeumo, played through by Cunha for a one-on-one with Vásquez, saw his shot hit one post and then the other one before refusing to cross the line. United threatened from corners. Maguire went close. Dalot had a header cleared off the line.

The United support had endured that familiar wrestle before kick-off; trying to find hope in face of the negativity, the deep sense of foreboding. Kobbie Mainoo’s return to the starting XI provided a glimmer. He was in the mood to make his moves.

Carrick’s major selection decision was to start Heaven over Lisandro Martínez in central defence. It shone a light into Martínez’s current headspace. It is a dark place. Martínez would get on for Heaven towards the end.

United fought. It was shocking to see how Roma, unbeaten so far this season in Serie A, fell apart. Cunha made the difference. United deal only in the craziest of extremes.

items.lbText:
Defender expected to keep place after red card at Chelsea

Martínez’s ‘commitment is not an issue’, says Carrick

Michael Carrick has insisted he is not concerned about Lisandro Martínez’s attitude despite the defender’s recent outburst aimed at the Manchester United hierarchy which was then followed by his reckless sending off in the defeat against Chelsea at the weekend.

Martínez, who was fined for his comments about United’s director of football , Jason Wilcox, is expected to keep his place for the visit of Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday as United aim to end their worst run in 38 years, having failed to win any of their past nine matches.

“I’ve got no concerns about commitment at all,” Carrick said of the Argentina World Cup winner. “Things happen in football, sometimes you do things, sometimes you make a decision, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes it goes well for you, but the commitment is not an issue.”

Away defeats against Atlético Madrid and Como have left United’s 21st in the Champions League league phase, with it felt that Carrick needs a positive result against Roma, as well as against Aston Villa in the Premier League on Sunday, to keep his job. Martínez is suspended for the visit of Unai Emery’s men following his red card at Stamford Bridge.

“I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s going to happen,” Carrick insisted. “That doesn’t change the way I feel, that’s how we’re preparing for the game tomorrow and I’m really looking forward to the game.

“You might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had and what’s going on, but I genuinely can’t wait for the game tomorrow and that’s all I’m focused on. Whatever happens is going to happen after that, in whatever direction it goes in.”

United’s most recent home game was the 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth, which concluded with the players being booed by the Stretford End. “In these tough times you can’t expect the fans 100,000% of the time to be happy and cheering when we’re not putting out results,” Kobbie Mainoo said. “We owe it to them to put the results out there for them to cheer again.

“I feel like our way to repay that [the manager’s support] is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it and fight for us and fight for us as a team.”

Carrick will be without Luke Shaw, Marcus Rashford and Benjamin Sesko for the visit of Roma, while Patrick Dorgu has returned to training but is not fit enough to take part.

items.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Marco Rose’s tactics are lifting Bournemouth, Roméo Lavia makes progress with Chelsea and Roberto De Zerbi gives youth a chance at Spurs

Good defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0. Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Marco Rose’s tactics are lifting Bournemouth, Roméo Lavia makes progress with Chelsea and Roberto De Zerbi gives youth a chance at Spurs

Good defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0 . Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team. John Brewin

No shots on target for Liverpool , leaving them with zero margin for the errors that preceded Kai Havertz’s decisive goal. Nine points behind Arsenal with a quarter of the season gone, Liverpool’s season risks becoming a developmental one, a time to regroup and rethink rather than challenging for the title. The squad Iraola inherited still bears the weight of the failed rebuild of the summer of 2025. Florian Wirtz was both unlucky when rattling the crossbar and too ponderous when a second-half chance dropped his way. Alexander Isak is nothing like the busy-bee striker his manager asks to press from the front. Milos Kerkez continues to be chaotic. Bradley Barcola, 2026’s headline signing, played his part in the flurry that followed Arsenal’s goal but faded, as did his fellow forwards. There are shards of light. Jérémy Jacquet and Trey Nyoni (aggressive – perhaps too aggressive – and involved in his hour on the field) are young players who can go places. Though it may take some time for Liverpool to get there as a team. JB

The small matter of a glamorous trip to Barcelona comes first for Aston Villa but it is a quirk of timing that Unai Emery’s next Premier League assignment should come at Old Trafford. It is the historical stature of Manchester United that triggered all the controversy over Jamie Carragher’s claim that Emery should be looking to climb the football chain and consider succeeding Michael Carrick should he be sacked. But even if Emery perceived United as a step up (as Youri Tielemans did when trading clubs in the summer , and look where that’s led him), would he prosper there? At Villa Park, he has an increasingly strong hold on how all team affairs are run, as signalled by his nominal upgrade from head coach to manager when he last signed a new contract, and he will visit the Camp Nou looking to extend Villa’s 100% start to their Champions League campaign. Having suffered dips at Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal, there is no certainty Emery’s methods would work in the febrile cauldron that is Old Trafford. After all, Manchester United will never be Aston Villa. Peter Lansley

Bournemouth are in full flow, winning each of their past six matches, scoring 16 goals. All while Alex Scott is absent with the muscle injury sustained with England. Those goals have come unanswered. Marco Rose has added a defensive solidity not always present during Iraola’s era. Last season’s goal difference was +4. Djordje Petrovic has not conceded a goal since the 5-1 defeat at Chelsea on 10 October. “The Chelsea game was the moment we changed all momentum,” said Petrovic after beating Leeds. Rose has admitted testing opening weeks in the Premier League had altered perceptions to force a rethink. “Everyone in the team, starting from the attackers, is doing their job offensively and defensively,” he said. Since Stamford Bridge, commitment to the collective has paid impressive dividends. “If you have that intensity with the attackers, it gets easier,” said Petrovic. “We have a good group of players with quality and huge rotations in each position.” J B

Roméo Lavia completed his first 90 minutes as a Chelsea player during their Carabao Cup defeat by Liverpool last Wednesday. It was a major milestone for a player who has struggled to stay fit since joining from Southampton three years ago. Lavia’s injury record invites caution but the midfielder is making progress. He followed up his performance against Liverpool with his second consecutive 90-minute display when Chelsea beat Manchester United 2-0 on Saturday. “As long as I feel good, I’ll do everything possible to help the team to get this type of result and I’m feeling good, so I’m very happy with my performance,” Lavia said after starring against United and creating the opening goal for Morgan Rogers. “All I can say is that the work that we’re doing with all the people at the club is going well. It’s just about keeping it going. Hopefully it can continue this way.” Jacob Steinberg

With Tottenham cruising towards a third successive Premier League victory , against 10-man Crystal Palace, Roberto De Zerbi decided the time had come in the 88th minute. Luca Williams-Barnett is rated as one of the best prospects to emerge from the Spurs academy in many years but the attacking midfielder has had to be patient for his first league appearance as De Zerbi’s side struggled at the start of the season. The 18-year-old made an instant impression with a sensational first touch and pass after replacing Mathys Tel before setting up Mohammed Kudus for a great chance, to make it 3-0, that was spurned. We can expect to see more of him if De Zerbi gets his way. “My career is clear: when I have young, talented players, nothing changes,” he said. “I thought it was the right moment for him in the Premier League – but as a quality, he’s a big, big talent.” Ed Aarons…

items.title: Should Premier League strugglers stick or twist as pressure on managers mounts? | Andrew Beasley
items.author: Andrew Beasley
items.content:
Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far away

No Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change.

The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far away

No Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change.

The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away.

Michael Carrick remains the favourite to be the next manager to leave his post. He is unsurprisingly followed by the managers of the clubs who occupy the relegation zone: Pierre Sage of Crystal Palace, Sunderland’s Régis Le Bris and Oliver Glasner at Nottingham Forest . It seems almost inevitable that Carrick will leave soon so the more interesting analysis lies among the bottom three.

Sunderland sit 20th and are predicted by Opta to finish there. However, they have had a testing start to the season. Le Bris’s side have faced five of the current top seven clubs, the joint-most along with Liverpool. The manager also has enormous reserves of goodwill after taking the club back to the Premier League and then into Europe.

Despite their tough schedule, Sunderland came into the weekend within one expected point of Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham before losing 3-1 at Coventry with the xG count 1.8 to 0.7 in their favour. It was a familiar outcome for a side that has scored 6.2 goals fewer than expected this season.

With Sunderland’s next five league opponents being Chelsea, Aston Villa, Tottenham, Liverpool and Newcastle, the challenge of staying up will not immediately get easier. At least their chance‑converting woes are not as bad as those of Nottingham Forest.

Their shots have been worth 14.7 expected goals, the fourth most in the division after the matches on Saturday. But not once in a game this season have the goals they scored at least equalled their xG, let alone surpassed it. It is a finishing issue, not a question of opposition goalkeepers having super-human performances against them.

The analytical step above standard expected goals is xG on target (xGOT). It measures the likelihood of an on-target shot becoming a goal based on chance quality and shot placement. Forest’s xGOT this season is 7.4, little more than half of their expected goal tally.

This inability to test goalkeepers severely enough explains why Glasner’s men have scored just six times. They are squandering almost one goal per game on average according to their expected goals, a significant shortfall. None of the 96 teams in Europe’s big five leagues were worse than 0.5 goals per match below xG last season, which suggests Forest’s luck should turn for the better.

Is Evangelos Marinakis patient enough for that to happen? Forest’s expected goal data is much stronger for Glasner than it was under any of the four managers their owner fired last season. Whether he pays attention to such numbers is a different issue.

Glasner hinted at a physical deficiency in the squad after defeat at Brentford. “We are outrun by the opposition in every single game. We have to change it,” he said . Distance covered data from Fotmob suggests that is not quite the case, albeit Forest have been outrun in their past five league games. Both the underlying xG data and physical statistics are worse at Glasner’s former club Crystal Palace though.

As expected goals have a far greater bearing on future performance or results than running stats, those numbers are the greater concern. Equally, Palace’s average of 96.9 sprints per match is the fewest in the Premier League (after Saturday’s matches).

The club have been through similar teething troubles with new managers before. Palace’s previous two appointments that occurred between seasons were Frank de Boer and Patrick Vieira. The former was sacked after only five matches in all competitions in 2017, the latter won just one of his first nine league games four years later before recovering to finish 12th.

While Palace are a little wasteful in attack, they have not been as bad as Forest or Sunderland. Their defence is a much bigger problem, which is unusual as Sage’s Lens conceded the fourth fewest expected goals in Ligue 1 last season. Palace are second worst for that metric in the Premier League in 2026‑27, rock bottom if penalties are excluded. Some of that may be down to starting seven combinations of players in the back three because of injuries and Axel Disasi’s three‑match ban, but it is imperative that a manager overcomes such inevitable difficulties.

Palace host Liverpool next weekend. They return after the international break with potentially winnable games against Coventry and Hull. Will those fixtures represent a good opportunity for Sage to kickstart his reign or an excellent chance for his replacement to hit the ground running? Only the chair, Steve Parish, will know the answer but Palace are the strugglers who look most in need of managerial change.

items.lbText:
United 17th in Premier League after Chelsea defeat

No change expected until international break

Michael Carrick is set to remain in charge of Manchester United for Tuesday’s Champions League game against Roma at Old Trafford despite Saturday’s 2-0 loss at Chelsea.

The defeat means United have not won in nine games and have made their poorest start to a season since 1988, but Carrick’s position is expected to be reviewed again during the international break after the next round of Premier League matches, in which United host Aston Villa next Sunday.

The 45-year-old came close to losing his job last Monday when Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada met at the training ground to discuss his future. The director of football and the chief executive decided Carrick should be given a chance to turn form and results around.

Carrick’s side are in 17th with seven points, above the relegation zone only on goal difference.

There remains a view within the hierarchy that Carrick can still transform fortunes, with United’s travelling support still backing him at the end of the defeat at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

After the game the head coach indicated that he expected to still be in position for the Roma game. He said: “We’ve got to move forward and win matches, it’s as simple as that.”

Eddie Howe is Wilcox’s preferred candidate should Carrick be sacked, with contact between the parties understood to have been made. The former Newcastle ­manager is open to taking up the position, ­subject to negotiations. He would cost about £3m in compensation to Newcastle.

Julian Nagelsmann, the ­former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach, is highly regarded by ­Christopher ­Vivell, United’s director of ­recruitment, who is believed to have sounded out his fellow ­German. The pair previously worked together at RB Leipzig.

items.title: Manchester United’s capitulation at Chelsea paints picture of a club that barely exists | Barney Ronay
items.author: Barney Ronay at Stamford Bridge
items.content:
Michael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual story

On and on and on. And then on just a little bit more it would seem. Manchester United: always crashing in the same Carrick.

The obvious question after this 2-0 defeat against Chelsea is how much longer United will continue to lose games under the current manager, as opposed to losing games under the next one. But it is also a mark of the dysfunction of this club, its ambient levels of sadness, that this matters so little.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Michael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual story

On and on and on. And then on just a little bit more it would seem. Manchester United: always crashing in the same Carrick.

The obvious question after this 2-0 defeat to Chelsea is how much longer United will continue to lose games under the current manager, as opposed to losing games under the next one. But it is also a mark of the dysfunction of this club, its ambient levels of sadness, that this matters so little.

Here we have another staging point in the progress of the Manchester United ghost ship, where even sacking a manager carries almost zero tension, where it feels like something that has basically already happened. This is a club that can make you into a relic of the past even while you’re still walking around taking training and drawing a salary.

Michael Carrick is miles away from being the actual story here. For the record, the United manager is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, pretty much already lounging around in one of those holiday adverts with Tony Pulis joshing about what’s for lunch. This defeat means United haven’t won a game since early September. At full time only the fact that Coventry and Sunderland would be playing each other later in the afternoon ruled out the prospect of an end-of-day bottom place.

Chuck in a Carabao Cup exit and 20th spot in the Champions League mega-table. Troubled times, then, for the latest semi-permanent navy wool suit in the United dugout. Something will now happen, most likely Carrick’s removal once the appropriate replacement is lined up. What happened here was almost by the by. Although it still provided some pretty vivid evidence of where this club is.

If there was a key moment, it arrived with 48 minutes gone and the score still 0-0. At which point Morgan Rogers scored a goal that captured entirely what Manchester United is. In real time, this felt like one of those football moments, where the metaphor, the symbolism is almost too much, the nudge in the ribs a little too hard.

Rogers took the ball on the edge of the centre circle and just kept running in a straight line through sudden empty spaces where there should have been a thing called Manchester United. Instead he found an anti-United, a non-United. Manchester United as an absence. So much analysis of this club evolves around what is it for, where should it turn, what can it be? Maybe it’s not really anything at all.

We do remember Manchester United. It has a cultural memory, a set of shapes and colours, a gripping centre. Or does it? There was once a dream that was Manchester United. You could whisper its name. Anything more than a whisper and it would vanish. So Rogers just kept running in a straight line, moving fast now, finding no resistance, nothing of substance, fibre, no flesh, no will in front of him, like opening up the curtains and watching the shadows disappear.

How many times has this happened at this level, that a player is able to take the ball and run 40 yards through a packed opposition half without having to dribble, beat a player or even swerve around some tangible object?

This is not to diminish Rogers’s skill and drive. The finish was really nice, a little dink as Senne Lammens came out and made a strange shape, as confused as anyone else by the sudden appearance of a living, moving, actual human in front of him.

Teams are often described as having been found out, their patterns solved and learned. It turns out this is the way to score against Manchester United. Just run straight through the middle of them.

Before long it was time for Lisandro Martínez to get sent off, again playing football that wasn’t really there. Chelsea took a corner from the right. At which point Martínez rammed his arm into Wesley Fofana’s neck with the ball miles away. Maybe Martínez just wanted to touch another human being. Sometimes you just need to feel something.

Cole Palmer buried the penalty to make the score 2-0, with United a man down and not existing, just a little bit more. And OK, OK, you’re still thinking about the good news, aren’t you? Well, presumably Sir Jim Ratcliffe will see the material gain here, the chance to save on hotel costs with another nonexistent team. No, we don’t need any rooms. We are non-corporeal.

On a more positive note, at least the players are annoyed. Really. It has been seen as a sign of dysfunction, the ravens leaving the tower, that United’s senior players have begun to speak in public. But wouldn’t it be weird if they didn’t? What is the correct human response to this state of complete, top-down lack of care, of managed disintegration?

The first half was lively enough. Bruno Fernandes was back in the United starting XI on a lovely crisp October morning, the sun sharp but soft, the grass a deep lime green. It is said that United lack leaders. But what is a leader? Someone who shows you how to win, makes winning more likely, walks you right to the door. Well, good luck with that around here. The sub-Saharan desert also lacks grass. This isn’t really the fault of grass.

And so Manchester United started with one bloke who thinks the hierarchy has betrayed the club and another who thinks the manager is tactically poor. The thing is, they’re both right. Fernandes in particular broke the code, undermining his manager , talking tactics when you are housefly playing like a performatively unhappy jack russell.

But it is hard to blame the players too much for losing the run of themselves a little. This is a club that takes a bite out of everyone, that makes everything wrong, a club that spends and spends and still seems short, that is somehow ludicrously profitable, but also ludicrously in debt, where to be a supporter is to be left always feeling short-changed, owed so much more.…

items.lbText:
Defeat against Chelsea extends winless run to nine games

Carrick clinging on to job after club’s worst run since 1988

Michael Carrick insisted he would still be in charge when Manchester United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, despite the 2-0 defeat at Chelsea on Saturday. United’s problems mounted as their winless run reached nine games . Carrick is clinging on to his job after overseeing the club’s first such run since 1988 and tried to focus on the next game as he analysed his side’s defending when Morgan Rogers opened the scoring for Chelsea.

“It’s never a good goal to concede,” he said. “Morgan went through the middle of us and at that point the game was right in the balance. To concede like that was a big moment. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

United played well during the first half, but missed a series of clear opportunities. They folded after going behind and their fate was sealed when Lisandro Martínez was sent off for a foul that led to Cole Palmer making it 2-0 from the spot. Carrick, though, steered clear of criticising one of his most experienced players for leaving United in the lurch.

“It was a major part of the game,” he said. “The second goal and losing the man at that stage had a big influence on it.”

United were just above the bottom three before the afternoon games, but Carrick said there would be no stigma attached to one of the biggest clubs in the country falling into the relegation zone should results elsewhere have that effect. “There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes it any different,” he said. “It’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches, it’s as simple as that.”

Carrick was asked if his players were ready for a relegation battle. “You can look at it like that, and you can look at how far you can move up the league quite quickly if you win football matches,” he said. “That’s the way it’s got to be approached.”

Chelsea moved into fourth place overnight, responding well to losing to Tottenham in the league and Liverpool on penalties in the Carabao Cup. “The first half was intense,” Xabi Alonso said. “United had their chances, we were close as well, so at half-time we have spoken and the reaction from the second half was better.

“We started quite well, we got the lead, we looked in better control and after 2-0 and the red card the context of the game changed. But it has not been easy.”

Alonso praised Estêvão Willian after the Brazil winger sparkled on his first start in the league this season. “We spoke after Tottenham and he knew that he was going to be playing today,” the Chelsea manager said. “He has had the best response to show he deserves more, that he was prepared and that’s what you want, so I’m very happy for him.”

items.lbText:
Get ready for another week of agonising over the sorry state of Manchester United . The legends of old will rage, clips of a fuming Gary Neville will fly around social media, the airwaves will reverberate with complaints from angry supporters and by the time United play again there is every chance a new manager will be in the dugout.

There were echoes of Erik ten Hag’s final game in charge as the walls closed in on Michael Carrick at Stamford Bridge. United missed a series of golden chances when the scores were level, just as they did when Ten Hag lost to West Ham a day before his sacking two years ago, and Chelsea made the most of the reprieve after initially delivering a performance so bad it had you worrying for the nascent Xabi Alonso project.

Chelsea could not have been worse during the first half. It helped that their opponents were in a giving mood. United had opportunities to make their decision to give Carrick a stay of execution look like a wise move rather than the consequence of executive level confusion, but their finishing was awful and their defending even worse. They watched as Morgan Rogers breezed through to make it 1-0 early in the second half and their seventh defeat in 13 games was sealed when Lisandro Martínez earned a red card for giving away the penalty that allowed Cole Palmer to push Chelsea into fourth place.

It symbolised United’s decline under the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Martínez has had a lot to say recently , but the Argentinian should have been sold long ago. That he is yet to go sums up United’s shoddy recruitment. They are carrying so much deadwood and it is hard to see their problems being fixed by a change of manager. Carrick is merely one of many issues. He will probably have gone by the time United face Roma on Tuesday and whoever takes over will inherit a team sleepwalking into a relegation battle.

This is not a happy ship. The ending was similar to last week’s defeat to Bournemouth . Carrick was applauded when he walked over at full-time. They sang his name and booed when the United players made a sheepish trudge to the away end at full time.

The spotlight was also on Alonso, defeats to Tottenham in the league and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup sparking criticism over team selections, and he lifted his side by handing Estêvão Willian his first start in the league this season.

Overlooked at Anfield, Estêvão was dangerous on the right flank after Alonso adjusted without the injured João Pedro up front. Pedro Neto rather than Danny Welbeck led the line in a 4-2-3-1 system but it was United who threatened first. Diogo Dalot combined with Mateus Cunha on the left and Andrey Santos, who left Chelsea for United last summer, swept a shot just wide from 20 yards.

Both sides brought vulnerabilities to the table. Chelsea had a long list of absentees – illness ruled Jordan Henderson out in midfield – and their defence wobbled without Maxence Lacroix. United, though not exactly secure whenever Chelsea punched through on the counterattack, felt optimistic at first.

The visitors had an escape when Senne Lammens spilled a Neto shot and an offside Estêvão tapped home but Carrick was the happier manager during the first half. Fernandes, back after clear the air talks with Carrick, shimmered in a floating role from the left. Bryan Mbeumo and Cunha were lively, although the worry for United was making their dominance count.

Fernandes was wasteful at the end of a flowing counterattack, firing over from Mbeumo’s pass. Amad Diallo, dangerous against Marco Palestra, cut inside to fire two efforts on target and Chelsea, enjoying neither possession nor control against Santos and Carlos Baleba, were forced into emergency mode.

Levi Colwill intervened when Cunha broke through and Wesley Fofana took flak from the home fans after a couple of trademark brain farts. Mbeumo and Diallo missed after mistakes by the Frenchman, though it is worth stressing that a dismal half from Chelsea was a team effort. They were lucky when Cunha had what would have been the opening goal disallowed by the video assistant referee (VAR) for offside.

The away end ran through the anti-board chants – urging the Glazers to sell up and questioning Jason Wilcox’s credentials as technical director – and United feared being punished for their profligacy. There were a couple of flashes from Chelsea; Moisés Caicedo diverted a Fofana header against the woodwork and Neto shot wide after a stumble from Harry Maguire.

Chelsea were more assertive at the start of the second half and it was easy to predict United’s unravelling. They were punished when Mbeumo turned into trouble in midfield. Caicedo blocked his path, Roméo Lavia nicked the ball past Baleba and Rogers took over. Facing no resistance, the £117m man’s saunter through the middle placed United’s failure to strengthen in defence into sharp focus.

It was a bit like a goal you see at the end of a casual five-a-side between a group of dads playing for the first time since 2019. Maguire barely lifted a leg, Martínez gawped and Rogers dinked over Lammens for 1-0.

The challenge for United was to dig deep, to stand tall. Good luck with that. Lavia was running the midfield for Chelsea now.

There was a sense of the players in red giving up when Martínez elbowed Fofana at a corner. The Argentinian was already on a booking and he was off when Peter Bankes reviewed the incident, leaving Palmer to put United’s 10 men to bed by making it 2-0 from the spot.

Saturday’s meeting at Stamford Bridge could be pivotal for both Xabi Alonso and Carrick. Chelsea and Manchester United aren’t where they want to be and this encounter will give a sense of their chances of changing that.

Without João Pedro, Chelsea have struggled for attacking fluency in their last two games. Alonso has used Morgan Rogers and Emmanuel Emegha as deputy No 9s without success, which could point to Danny Welbeck starting against his former club on Saturday.

Manchester United are similarly struggling for attacking fluency, as well as defensive solidity, midfield control and a general sense of a dressing room fighting for their manager. What was widely expected to be the first match of the post-Carrick era is now another chance for the 45-year-old to turn things around.

United are winless in their last eight matches in all competitions while Chelsea have kept just one clean sheet in eight Premier League outings. All points to this match being a volatile one that could swing either way.

Player to watch: Morgan Rogers, Chelsea – Perhaps lucky not to be sent off against Tottenham Hotspur, Rogers has registered five goal contributions in just eight league games for Chelsea. The England international will pose a threat in and around the opposition area.

items.lbText:
Head coach reflects on ‘not always rosy’ conversations

Players ‘hurting’ after eight games without a win

Michael Carrick said he has had difficult conversations with the Manchester United hierarchy and his players during their turbulent start to the season.

United have not won in their past eight games and start the weekend in 16th place of 20 in the league, one point above the relegation zone.

Carrick’s position was under threat after losing last Sunday to Bournemouth but he has held on to his job for the time being and been given the chance to turn things around, starting at Chelsea on Saturday.

The head coach suggested he had spoken with the club’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the chief executive, Omar Berrada, this week.

“It’s pretty clear, it’s not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that’s between me and the players, whether that’s between me, Jason, Omar or the owners,” Carrick said. “It’s the truth, it’s the hard truth at times and it’s what we need to move forward. Whatever we need to move forward, we will do.”

The supporters cheered Carrick off after he did a lap of the pitch in the aftermath of Sunday’s 3-0 defeat , but once he entered the tunnel they booed the players after a poor performance and perceived lack of effort. Carrick said the players are “hurting” but are “hungry” to turn things around.

“I’ll be totally honest, it was mixed feelings for me,” Carrick said. “To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.

“It wasn’t a nice situation but to feel that was important, of course, but it didn’t make me feel better in the fact that I’m with the players 100% and we’re all in it together. I’ve told the players that, I’m happy to say that.

“I didn’t feel comfortable being in any way, shape or form, a separation from that. That’s my group, my players and this is my football club so we have to all be in it together, and that’s the supporters included. As hard as it is at the moment, I totally get that, I get their feelings, but when we get through this then we’ll be a lot stronger as a whole.”

Gary Neville questioned some of the players’ professionalism on his podcast this week. “I’ve got no time for them,” Neville said. “There’s a few of them that don’t go to bed at the right time. Don’t eat the right things.” Carrick laughed off the allegations with the remark: “Gaz says a lot of things.”
